title: Constant-factor universally truthful auctions for submodular bidders
area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
formal:
Does there exist a universal constant \(C\ge1\) and one uniform randomized combinatorial-auction mechanism with polynomial worst-case communication which is universally truthful and, for every number \(n\ge1\) of bidders, number \(m\ge1\) of items, public precision bound \(B\ge1\), and admissible normalized monotone submodular valuation profile \(v\), satisfies
\[\mathbb E_r\!\left[\sum_{i=1}^n v_i(S_i(v;r))\right]
\ \ge\ \frac{\operatorname{OPT}(v)}{C}?\]
The constant is independent of \(n,m,B\). The expectation is over report-independent mechanism randomness. For each fixed random realization the allocation and payment rule must satisfy the dominant-strategy inequality below. Communication is measured in bits, with unlimited terminating local computation and arbitrary interactive messages, including demand queries.
definitions:
Items and types. Let \([m]=\{1,\ldots,m\}\). Bidder \(i\) privately holds the entire function \(v_i:2^{[m]}\to\mathbb Q_{\ge0}\). It is normalized, monotone and submodular: for all subsets \(S,T\subseteq[m]\),
\[v_i(\varnothing)=0,\qquad S\subseteq T\Longrightarrow v_i(S)\le v_i(T),\]
\[v_i(S)+v_i(T)\ge v_i(S\cup T)+v_i(S\cap T).\]
The public integer \(B\ge1\) bounds each value separately: every value admits a representation \(p/q\) with integers \(0\le p<2^B\), \(1\le q<2^B\). Write \(\mathcal V_{m,B}\) for this domain. Different bidders may have completely different functions in the domain. Their full tables have \(2^m\) entries each and are private local inputs, not publicly supplied data. There is no oracle promise, common valuation, eligibility graph, prior distribution, budget or succinct representation requirement on the types. The domain of an alternative reported valuation is also \(\mathcal V_{m,B}\), with the same public parameters.

Outcomes and utilities. A feasible allocation is \(a:[m]\to\{0,1,\ldots,n\}\), with zero meaning unallocated. Bidder \(i\) receives \(S_i=\{j:a(j)=i\}\); bundles are pairwise disjoint and no item is split. Each bidder has a finite rational payment \(p_i\in\mathbb Q\), with positive sign meaning money paid to the auctioneer. Its utility is \(v_i(S_i)-p_i\). No individual-rationality, budget-balance or transfer-sign condition is added. For a true profile \(v=(v_1,\ldots,v_n)\), define
\[W_v(a)=\sum_{i=1}^n v_i(S_i),\qquad
\operatorname{OPT}(v)=\max_{a:[m]\to\{0,\ldots,n\}}W_v(a).\]
The finite maximum exists. Welfare measures bidder values only; it excludes payments and auctioneer revenue. Zero valuations and zero optimum are allowed. All bidders are evaluated using their true values at the final allocation.

Communication model. The auctioneer and bidders run a common uniform protocol on distributed reported types. Local algorithms are ordinary finite programs, with unrestricted computation on their private tables; all local computations and protocol executions must terminate. The auctioneer initially knows only \(n,m,B\). A public blackboard holds the transcript; each transmitted bit counts once. The next speaker and the decision to halt are determined by the public transcript, public parameters and fixed random tape. Private computation time and silent delays are not messages or additional information channels. The output allocation and all payments are written to the transcript and count toward its length. Any use of private channels can instead be specified with sender and recipient information and charged in the transcript.

Rational values, prices and payments are communicated exactly as finite binary numerator/positive-denominator pairs, with a sign bit when needed and self-delimiting integer encodings. For example, for \(z\ge0\), use \(1^\ell0\operatorname{bin}(z+1)\), where \(\ell\) is the bit length of \(z+1\). Subsets can be transmitted by their \(m\)-bit incidence vectors. Every query description, price, reply, routing description and final output is charged. A value query specifies a bidder and a bundle and receives its value. A demand query specifies rational item prices \((\pi_j)_{j\in[m]}\) and receives a bundle maximizing \(v_i(S)-\sum_{j\in S}\pi_j\). Any deterministic tie rule needed to define the mechanism is part of the protocol. Solving that finite optimization locally has no time charge, but sending its prices and answer does. These are examples of allowed messages, not an exhaustive query restriction.

Polynomial communication and randomness. There must exist constants \(K>0\) and \(d\in\mathbb N\) such that the total number of transmitted bits is at most \(K(n+m+B+1)^d\) for every valid reported profile and every realization of the mechanism’s random bits. This is worst-case communication, not expected communication and not merely a query count. Randomness is a public tape of independent fair bits, independent of all types and reports; its use and local computation are uncharged, although execution still terminates. The uniform protocol describes how those bits are used. Fixing the tape \(r\) defines a deterministic allocation and payment rule \((S(v;r),p(v;r))\).

Universal truthfulness. For every public parameter triple, every fixed \(r\), bidder \(i\), true and alternative reported types \(v_i,w_i\in\mathcal V_{m,B}\), and other reported profile \(b_{-i}\in\mathcal V_{m,B}^{n-1}\), require
\[v_i(S_i(v_i,b_{-i};r))-p_i(v_i,b_{-i};r)
\ \ge\ v_i(S_i(w_i,b_{-i};r))-p_i(w_i,b_{-i};r).\]
Both sides use the same true valuation and random tape. The protocol implements this direct-report outcome rule without transmitting the full reported tables. There is no averaging in the incentive condition; averaging is used only in the welfare guarantee. No assumption that other bidders are honest, no prior over their values, and no weakening to Bayesian or truthful-in-expectation incentives is permitted.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the existence claim or its negation. A positive answer must specify the uniform protocol, payment rule and randomization, a fixed approximation constant and a fixed polynomial communication bound. Prove feasibility, termination, all-bit accounting, the incentive inequality for every fixed random tape, and the expected welfare bound for every admissible profile.

A negative answer must rule out every fixed constant and every protocol in the full model, including arbitrary interactive messages, demand queries and unlimited local computation. Failure of one mechanism or one prescribed approximation constant does not refute existence of another. A lower bound restricted to value queries, deterministic mechanisms, a particular family of allocation rules, or polynomial local time alone is insufficient.

Truthfulness in expectation alone, approximate incentives, a factor growing with \(m\), an uncharged exponential price description, or a constant guarantee with extra valuation promises does not meet the target. Conditional impossibility results must keep their hypotheses explicit and do not by themselves refute this unconditional communication claim. The target is expected welfare; a stronger high-probability guarantee is welcome but not required.
why: Determine whether exact truthful incentives inherently cause an unbounded loss of allocative efficiency, even when arbitrary compact communication and unlimited local optimization are available.

importance.reason: A central multi-parameter mechanism-design problem linking truthful incentives, submodular optimization, information elicitation and the communication cost of welfare approximation.

progress.text: Dobzinski–Dughmi distinguish universal truthfulness from truthfulness in expectation and separate their power in a restricted multi-unit setting.
Dobzinski proves exponential value-query requirements for universally truthful \(m^{1/2- \varepsilon}\)-approximation; arbitrary communication remains outside this lower bound.
Assadi–Singla obtain expected \(O((\log\log m)^3)\) approximation with universal truthfulness and polynomially many queries.
Assadi–Kesselheim–Singla improve the submodular and XOS factor to \(O((\log  \log  m)^{2})\); Theorem 2 uses at most n value and demand queries.
Christodoulou–Koutsoupias–Kovács–Vlachos establish constant truthful guarantees under graph eligibility restrictions, without solving unrestricted submodular auctions.
The budget-feasible procurement preprint has a different private-cost model; its constant claim is not a general welfare-auction mechanism.

status_note: Checked on 16 September 2026. The inspected general upper guarantee remains \(O((\log\log m)^2)\) with universal truthfulness and expected welfare. Value-query lower bounds do not cover arbitrary communication. The February 2026 graph-auction theorem and August procurement claims have distinct restrictions or type spaces. No matching constant-factor resolution was found in the bounded primary-source search; complete cited proofs were not independently formalized.

context_blocks.text: A bidder may value several items as substitutes. For example, a coverage valuation assigns each item a set of useful features and values a bundle by the total weight of features covered at least once. Receiving an item has less marginal value when many of its features are already covered. Submodularity abstracts this diminishing-returns property without requiring the valuation to be supplied as an explicit coverage instance.

The auctioneer must allocate the items using information held by strategic bidders. Maximizing the sum of their values is the social-welfare objective; maximizing the auctioneer’s revenue would be a different problem. Payments influence what information bidders choose to provide, but are transfers and do not enter the welfare objective. Even a very poor revenue guarantee would be acceptable here if incentives and welfare met the stated requirements.

Two established results cover separate parts of the requirements. With complete reports and unrestricted resources, the Vickrey–Clarke–Groves mechanism obtains optimal welfare and truthful incentives. If incentives are omitted, submodular welfare admits constant-factor approximation from compact queries. The difficulty is combining the guarantees while avoiding communication of exponentially many bundle values. The 2026 graph-auctions paper describes this communication perspective explicitly.

Universal truthfulness is a strong use of randomization: each mechanism obtained after fixing the coins must itself make truthful reporting optimal. Truthfulness in expectation requires only that the average utility discourage lying. The distinction has mathematical force; Dobzinski and Dughmi separate the two notions in a restricted multi-unit setting. Their separation is useful background, but their multi-unit approximation scheme does not supply a mechanism for arbitrary heterogeneous submodular valuations.

A demand answer can describe a preferred bundle in \(m\) bits even if finding it requires comparing exponentially many bundles. The price vector must also be sent and paid for in the communication bound. This explains why a communication-efficient mechanism can delegate difficult optimization to a bidder without being computationally efficient for that bidder. It also explains why a bound on the number of queries alone is not a complete bit-cost specification.

Dobzinski’s impossibility theorem rules out universally truthful \(m^{1/2- \varepsilon}\)-approximation using polynomially many value queries, for every fixed \(\varepsilon >0\). A value query reveals only one specified bundle’s value. The theorem is a genuine barrier in that access model, but it cannot be extended by simply treating a demand query as one more value query. A demand answer can encode the result of comparing exponentially many bundles.

Assadi and Singla’s FOCS 2019 result gives a universally truthful expected \(O((\log\log m)^3)\) welfare approximation with polynomially many queries. The later journal publication records the same advance, rather than a new constant-factor result. These approximation factors are asymptotic as the number of items grows.

Assadi, Kesselheim and Singla’s Theorem 2 improves the expected approximation factor for submodular and XOS bidders to \(O((\log\log m)^2)\), using at most one value or demand query per bidder. For the broader subadditive class the guarantee is \(O((\log\log m)^3)\). The theorem is universally truthful. The squared iterated logarithm still diverges, so it does not supply the fixed constant sought here.

Recent positive results for graph auctions restrict each item to a small set of eligible bidders. For example, the 2026 paper gives a truthful factor-two mechanism when each item has two eligible bidders and valuations are subadditive. This structural restriction supplies information absent in a general auction, so it does not settle the present question. A general constant-factor mechanism would show that exact incentive compatibility need not impose an unbounded welfare loss in this central communication model.

An August 2026 preprint claims constant budget-feasible approximations with demand queries. Its buyer purchases services from sellers with private participation costs under a payment budget. That is a different type space and objective from allocating items among bidders with private submodular bundle values. The result therefore does not resolve this card, even though both settings use truthfulness and submodularity.

sentences: The auction allocates indivisible items to bidders with private normalized monotone submodular bundle valuations.
The question asks for a constant expected-welfare approximation with universal truthfulness and polynomial communication in bidders, items and per-value bit precision.
Local computation is unrestricted, but every query description, price, reply, allocation and payment must fit the bit bound.
A complete Lean proof must establish the fixed-random-tape incentive inequality and all-profile welfare guarantee, or rule out every protocol in this full class.
Value-query impossibility, graph eligibility results, growing approximation factors and budget-feasible procurement do not settle the selected target.
